doc.title: Mandel Johnny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Los Angeles, Chet Baker and film beginnings
title: Jack Sheldon, Joe Mondragon and the gun
summary: Mandel tells a story of Mondragon pulling a gun after Jack Sheldon was punched, and discusses Mondragon's Apache heritage and Miles Davis.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I know, what a funny guy, he and Joe Maini used to work together and they were hysterical. I don’t know, I’m gonna tell a story on tape here. Joe Mondragon was my bass player for a long time, I just loved the way Joe Mondragon played. He and Jack Sheldon used to work a lot together and [laughs] I don’t know if this story belongs on this tape or not but it’s – they were playing a dance somewhere and Jack, you know Jack cannot stop with one-liners and there was

this girl who was more than fine at the dance and she was with her fiancé and Jack just kept zinging those one – he couldn't take his eyes off the girl, he couldn’t stop, he just couldn't leave her alone and the guy finally really started getting hot and he goes over to Jack and says, “Look this is my fiancé, this is the girl I’m going to marry, I’d really appreciate it,” he was very nice, “if you'd please stop, layoff.” And Jack couldn’t lay off, the night wore on, everybody got into their cups pretty well, finally Jack just went overboard and said something the guy hauls off and hits him square in the mouth and knocks him out. [laughs] And Dragon sees that and he runs, and this is the days before guns, he runs to his bass case and pulls out a gun, now I never saw Dragon with a gun before and in those days people didn't have guns, you know it wasn’t like that. You saw a gun that was very unusual and he goes up to the mic and starts waving it, and he says, “Alright you guys, everybody it's all over, the dance is finished everybody get out, everybody, get out stop the music the dance is finished,” and he turns to that guy, he says, “do you know what you did, you hit a trumpet player in the mouth, that is a mortal sin.”
[They both laugh]

He says, “All right everybody out,” I mean, you know he said, “I’d like to kill you, but you just don't realize what a terrible thing you did.” He said, “Everybody gets out, go on out of here,” and Jack is starting to come-to, and he opens one eye and he points, and he says, “She can stay.”
[They both laugh]
Okay, you can edit that out because it doesn’t really belong on the tape.
It’s a great story.
Yeah.
Well Joe Mondragon is part Indian right?
Yeah, not part, all.
All?
Yeah.
Well I…
Apache.
And part Mexican too right?
Well the Apache’s are that far south…
Yeah, yeah.
That I think that’s Mexican Indian really.
Don't mess with him.
No, what a wonderful man he was and what a great bass player.
Yeah, apparently he hipped Miles to the, “Concierto de Aranjuez,” you know the…
Yeah wouldn’t surprise me at all.
First, “Sketches of Spain,” he played Miles the original guitar recording and Miles loved it and played it for Gil, and that's where they got the idea to do it in, the “Sketches of Spain.”
I’m sorry I didn’t know Miles a lot better.
How well did you know him?
